speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Public Works):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF ADVISORY COMMISSION ON PARLIAMENTARY ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will doubtless remember that on July 20, 1973, I announced our intention of expropriating the land enclosed within Wellington, Elgin, Sparks and Bank streets in order that we might enlarge parliamentary facilities and protect the Parliament Hill environment. I also announced that we would try to get the co-operation of all parties of the House in creating an Advisory Commission on Parliamentary Accommodation to determine what facilities Parliament will need to operate efficiently in the future.
Since then, we have met the first requirements of the Expropriation Act and have made offers, as the fact requires, to all former owners. We are now studying, with them, the administrative steps to be taken to ensure the administration of real estate, and, especially, to make sure that the unique and attractive aspect of the Mall is preserved, an aspect on which I insisted in my previous statement.

Thanks to the co-operation of all parties, Mr. Speaker, I am in the happy position today to be able to announce the membership of the Advisory Commission on Parliamentary Accommodation. The commission will be comprised of members of all parties and both Houses and will include former distinguished parliamentarians. I trust that the Speakers of both Houses will accept to serve as ex officio members of the commission. The chairman will be a former cabinet minister and former Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, the Hon. Douglas C. Abbott. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will table after my brief statement the order in council and the names of the 16 members of the commission.
[DOT] (ino)
I believe all members will share my pleasure that we have been able to secure such distinguished participants to pursue this historic and important task on our behalf. It is vital that parliament, as the paramount legislative body of the nation, should be extended the full facilities it requires to perform effectively in this modern age. It is expected that in arriving at its conclusions the commission will look into how parliamentary needs should be met
in this country and compare with other countries with similar parliamentary institutions. Many complex problems about space, convenience, tradition and effectiveness will have to be faced and resolved by the commission on our behalf. The commission is being asked to look into these matters and to advise on the amount and type of accommodation and facilities, and how these will interrelate in order to permit parliament to operate effectively in the future.
The first stage in this process was the acquisition of the land and real estate and this has now been completed. The second stage is the one I just described, namely, the definition of the needs of parliament, as will be established by the advisory commission. The third stage will be the implementation, and I trust this will be facilitated by launching a competition open to all Canadian architects for providing the most inspiring concept of parliamentary architecture. This planning will be done in conjunction with the National Capital Commission and the city of Ottawa.
As I indicated in my earlier statement, the parliament of Canada is a vital symbol and presence in our country and we intend that its expansion will enhance and protect its dignity in accordance with the fundamental position it occupies in the life of the nation.
May I therefore, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the House, wish the commission full success in its deliberations.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF ADVISORY COMMISSION ON PARLIAMENTARY ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 20, 1973, when I spoke for the official opposition in reply to the minister's initial statement, I indicated at that time that we believe this project to be a significant development for parliament, and the calibre of the members of this special and important advisory commission honours the magnitude of the undertaking. The membership of the commission is a good balance between the various parties in the two chambers of parliament, but most important of all it represents, in the parliamentary sense, a good blend of experience on the one hand and freshness on the other.
We welcome reconfirmation of the intention to preserve the unique quality of the Sparks Street Mall which is important to the centre-town core of the national capital. We urge upon the minister, his department and the advisory commission the importance of consultation on a continuing basis with tenants and others who have an economic interest in that area because of the understandable uneasiness that can develop from an announcement of this kind.
I am sure that all of us urge upon the commission the importance of considering the changing role of the parliamentarian as one which is moving from the legislative on the one hand to a greater mixture of the legislative role and that of ombudsman on the other, where personal contact and frequent and direct communication are

April 26, 1974
becoming of increasing importance. I am sure that the commission will consult with serving members of parliament to ensure that the facilities are such that they can be adapted to these changes as they occur.
We welcome as well the aspect of competition for design to be limited to Canadian architects who, as a profession, are more than equal to this challenge. I hope there will be no unreasonable limitations placed on the ability of the commission to travel and to view innovations in legislative facilities throughout the world.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, the job of consultation and resolution of differences of opinion that will undoubtedly arise with local governmental authorities is a formidable one indeed, but we all share the view that this commission will be equal to that particular task. I should like to join with the hon. gentleman in wishing the commission every success.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF ADVISORY COMMISSION ON PARLIAMENTARY ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I had the privilege on July 20 of last year of responding to the statement made that day by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube). In doing so, I indicated the pleasure of this party with respect to the decision to appoint an advisory commission, the membership of which is now being made public. We welcome the progress that the government has now made concerning this matter in that it has proceeded with the expropriation arrangements.
I join with the Minister of Public Works and with the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) in wishing the very best to this commission. We are happy to have named two members of our party to it and we believe that they, along with others, will do a useful and imaginative job.
The fact is that the functions of members of parliament have multiplied greatly during the past few decades. Those of us who have been here for a while can testify to that fact. Even though we have not planned for change, we have had it. As the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton indicated, our functions as members of parliament include not only the legislative tasks that we have always had, even they are increasing; we have also become 264 ombudsmen, and it is important that the necessary facilities be made available so that these 264 ombudsmen can serve the interests of the people of Canada as a whole.
Every time this matter comes up I feel I must emphasize the desirability of realizing that this capital is not just an Ottawa institution, off somewhere removed from the rest of Canada, but that it belongs to all the people of this country. We can emphasize that by making it a place of beauty, and also by making it a place where the job that is supposed to be done is carried out. We must also, particularly in these days when there is so much more travel, increase the facilities for the visitors who come to this place. I am not thinking in terms of larger galleries so that more people can watch what is going on in this chamber. I am thinking of facilities for visitors in terms of increased committee space. I am thinking of facilities for people who come here to meet members to discuss their problems with their legislators and generally to express their concern about what goes on in their parliament which is, after all, what this institution is.

I urge that the commission keep in mind the desire that the Hill be a place of beauty as well as a place that is functional and efficient. I emphasize once again that I hope there will be sufficient co-operation among this commission, the National Capital Commission and the city of Ottawa so that the view of Parliament Hill will continue to be one that can be enjoyed from all parts of this city. I object very much to the way in which high-rise buildings are blotting out the view of this place which is, after all, important to the whole of Canada.
We welcome the announcement of the appointment of this commission and we wish its members well in the job they are undertaking.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF ADVISORY COMMISSION ON PARLIAMENTARY ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the statement of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube), and like those who spoke before me, I am pleased to see that two stages have been passed. There is one more to go and that is the realization of the wishes expressed last July.
Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the expropriations indicated in the statement will be carried out more fairly than has been the case at Ste. Scholastique. However, as a national capital, Ottawa must preserve a very distinctive character in this country. There are a great number of tourists, not only from Canada but from outside the country, who wish to see the capital. Ottawa is considered a national capital. I would feel then that Parliament is the first thing that attracts attention and the curiosity of visitors. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, the third stage, to implement the projects developed by the minister and this government, is most important. I point out, for example, the fact that those who come to Parliament to see their members have to be directed sometimes to another building, the West Block or Confederation Building.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the government and the minister should study the possibility of cleaning the central building to host all members of parliament, install air conditioning and appropriate offices, and transfer the senators to other buildings. As I see it, Parliament is indeed the Centre Block where we are now located and where all members of parliament should be.
The minister and the government should take measures to have all members of parliament located in the central Parliament building.

the question that was asked by the hon. member for Scarborough West. speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR INCORPORATION, OBJECTS, REGIONAL ADVISORY COUNCILS, POWERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, to incorporate the Federal Business Development Bank, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last July the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) announced in general terms some important measures to further encourage and assist the establishment and growth of Canadian small business. In order to implement these measures, Bill C-20 was tabled on April 8 to provide for the creation of a new Crown corporation which will bear the name Federal Business Development Bank. I am pleased, on behalf of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and for the government, to present this bill to the House today for second reading.
The new bank is the result of a careful assessment of the requirements of small business. This assessment has been based on the considerable experience which the government has gained with a wide range of programs designed to meet specific needs which it has introduced over the years. What the Federal Business Development Bank will do will be to combine a number of these programs, giving them new thrust and orientation, and provide a new organizational structure and guidelines under which they will be operated in a co-ordinated manner.
The new bank will provide a focal point for information, management counselling and training, and financing. Small businessmen who need information on government programs will find such information available in the branches of the bank. Those in need of management counselling to solve business problems will find it available at rates which they can afford. If financing is the requirement, small businessmen will find that loans are available under new flexible arrangements when such financing is not available on reasonable terms and conditions from the private sector. Moreover, the new bank will institute management seminars and, in general, provide

April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank
management training courses in conjunction with the provinces, universities and community colleges.
While the Federal Business Development Bank will bring together the necessary facilities to meet the main requirements of small business, it is not intended to meet all of them. When facilities outside the banks are required, the Federal Business Development Bank personnel will be able to refer clients to the sources of the additional help they may require and provide competent assistance to enable them to secure it.
In taking steps to create the Federal Business Development Bank, the government is primarily concerned with the needs of small business which are not being met by the private sector on terms and conditions that the small businessmen can accept. The intention is to supplement or complement these private services when, for one reason or another, they are not available to the small businessman.
The bank, Mr. Speaker, will be under instructions to encourage small business enterprises which have developed an appropriate degree of strength, to secure future financing and counselling services from the private sector.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, the three key elements in the philosophy behind the Federal Business Development Bank are: first, co-ordinated programs under independent management to meet the major needs of small business; second, the provision of a focal point where the small businessmen can find a competent person to talk to about his problems and requirements, and third, concentration on filling the gaps which exist in the private sector rather than competing with private institutions.
These elements are summed up in the objectives of the new bank which you will find set out in clause 4 of the bill, which reads as follows:
(X) The objects of the corporation are to promote and assist in the establishment and development of business enterprises in Canada by providing, in the manner and to the extent authorized by this act, financial assistance, management counselling, management training, information and advice and such other services as are ancillary or incidental to any of the foregoing.
(2) The corporation in carrying out its objects shall give particular consideration to the needs of small business enterprises.
In order to carry out these objectives, the new bank will require certain powers and an indication of how these powers should be used. With regard to financing operations, the legislation provides the bank with a full range of powers to enable it to meet any financial need of small business. It will be empowered to make or guarantee loans, to enter into underwriting agreements, to make equity investments and to engage in the financing of equipment and in leasing operations.
Great care has been taken in setting out the criteria under which these powers will be used. Financing is to be made available only when a person is engaged, or about to engage, in a business enterprise in Canada; when credit or other financial resources would not otherwise be available on reasonable terms and conditions; when the amount invested, or to be invested, in the enterprise by persons other than the bank, and the character of that investment, are such as to afford a reasonable expectation of a continuing commitment to the enterprise by such persons, and when the enterprise may reasonably be expected to prove successful.

The objective of the bank, coupled with powers and criteria for the financial services program is designed not only to enable the provision of financing when it is not available from the private sector on reasonable terms and conditions, but also to encourage private institutions to provide such financing. The decision on what are reasonable terms and conditions will be the responsibility of the board of the bank, as it is not possible to provide other than broad guidelines in the changing circumstances of the financial markets. While these powers are similar to those under which the Industrial Development Bank has operated successfully for many years, it is expected that the new bank will make fuller use of them.
For example, I expect that the new bank will give more careful consideration to the financial structure of small businesses and provide equity financing when this meets the financial and other needs of the client, such as extending the equity base to enable the firm to raise additional financing from private sources. With regard to term lending, no specific limitation is placed on the size of loan or size of business which may be financed, but general guidance is given that particular attention is to be paid to the needs of small business. Under similar guidelines, 77.4 per cent of the loans made by the Industrial Development Bank are for $50,000 or less, and the average authorization is now around $44,000. It is the government's intention that the Federal Business Development Bank concentrate its financing activities in the same way to meet the needs of small business.
The new bank will also introduce new and flexible lending techniques in recognition of the sometimes difficult financial situation of small businesses. For example, consideration will be given to delaying of repayment of principal for several years, arranging repayment schedules with balloon payments at maturity. These are only two of a number of new flexible techniques which I expect will improve financial services to small businessmen.
Mr. Speaker, members may recall that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stated on July 11 that the new bank would build on the existing strengths and organizational network of the Industrial Development Bank. This will indeed be the case. The Industrial Development Bank has, at present, 60 branch offices operating out of five regional offices. These will provide the initial office structure of the new bank. On the financial side, the Federal Business Development Bank will start from a strong financial base as the outstanding loans and commitments of the Industrial Development Bank total more than $800 million. Its clients currently number more than 19,000. Thus the new bank will begin its operations with a strong organization structure and a substantial clientele.
The new bank will have the power to provide management counselling services, directly or through others, to persons who are engaged in, or about to engage in, a business enterprise in Canada, who meet criteria established by the board, and when such services will supplement other available services from the private sector. The bank will have the power to underwrite the cost of providing counsellors when the requirements cannot be met by the bank's own staff.
April 26, 1974

The management counselling service will initially be provided by the Counselling Assistance to Small Enterprises, known as the CASE program, of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which program will be absorbed into the new bank. However, officers in all branches of the bank will be available to provide a sounding board for ideas developed by existing or prospective small businessmen to assist them in working out a viable idea that could be the basis of a commercial plan. Accordingly to need, the small businessman could then be directed to the appropriate source of information, expertise, or financing to meet his need. The bank will also have available counsellors who will provide detailed management advice in particular areas. This will be done initially by following the pattern already established by CASE in the use of retired executives as counsellors and by the use of private counsellors when retired executives are not in a position to deal with particular assignments. The CASE service is accordingly being expanded geographically in close consultation with the provinces, and the intention is to extend the coverage to the service sector in addition to the manufacturing and tourism sectors which are covered at present. As the bank gains experience in the area of management counselling, it will explore ways of improving, modifying and expanding these services.
In the management training field, the new bank will have the power to provide or enter into contracts with governments, agencies, associations or individuals for the provision of management training services. It will also be empowered to sponsor, support or organize conferences, seminars or other meetings for the promotion of good management practices.
In this area, the prime responsibility of the bank will be to pinpoint the needs of small business which can be filled most effectively by training and to meet those needs with the most effective training methods available. Consultation with provincial educational authorities, business associations, small businessmen and educational consultants, will all be necessary to ensure that training initiatives are appropriate, effective and complete. The training service will establish priorities, develop courses, or make contractual arrangements for the preparation of course materials by recognized experts and assist provincial government departments in the implementation processes. It will also play a useful role in developing and facilitating the exchange of information on implementation techniques, publicity, teacher training and other related teaching aids.
To fulfil these responsibilities initially, the bank will take over the owner/manager training program of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The relevant courses are short and oriented to specific aspects of small business management. The bank will also continue the one-day small business seminars provided by the Industrial Development Bank at different locations across Canada, with emphasis given to small cities, towns and remote areas where such services are not otherwise available.
The new bank will have the power to develop and operate an information service, publish and distribute information relative to the mandate of the bank, as well as to provide advice on federal programs for small business
Federal Business Development Bank and on assistance available to small business from others. To this end the bank will seek to establish close and continuing communication with provincial authorities.
This will be a major new thrust as the bank will act as a focal point for information on the wide range of federal services and programs designed to meet the needs of small business. The information services, to be provided locally through all offices of the bank, will be free to all interested persons and will be aimed at small firms that do not have the resources to seek out help from the multiplicity of specialized sources of assistance to small business- particularly those of the federal government. The services of the bank itself will also be made known more widely in this way. In addition to the immediate practical value to the inquirer, the information services will represent another two-way channel of communication between the businessman and the bank.
The activities of the information services will take several forms. The experienced local officers providing the services will give inquirers comprehensive information, competent advice and direct referral on the entire range of federal assistance programs and services for small business. The bank will provide reference libraries and booklets on a broad field of small business management subjects, and will publish and distribute industry profiles containing typical costs and operating date for specific industries. In this way, it will share with the public the experience gained by the bank and its predecessors in dealing with thousands of small businesses over many years. A Small Business News Bulletin, highlighting various assistance programs, business developments and many other forms of guidance to its readers, will be distributed to many thousands of small business operators.
In deciding on a corporate structure for the new bank, the government has had several considerations in mind. The first is that the new bank should have a considerable degree of independence in its day-to-day affairs. The second is that it should be guided by a strong top management that is well versed in business practice and representative of small business interests. These considerations have led to the decision to establish the Federal Business Development Bank as a proprietary corporation pursuant to Section 66 of the Financial Administration Act. It will report to Parliament on its activities through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie).
These same considerations were of importance in determining the number and composition of the board of directors. Ten of the fifteen directors will be chosen from the private sector to ensure broad business representation and access to business experience and expertise. To provide equitable geographic, cultural and population representation, two directors will be chosen from each of the five geographic regions of Canada. These members of the board will be appointed for a term of three years by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The remaining members of the board will be four senior federal officials and a full-time president who will also act as chief executive officer. A chairman, who will preside at meetings of the board, will be appointed by the board from among its members.

April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank
Provision is also made for an executive committee to deal with matters within the competence of the board when the latter is not in session. Its composition is outlined in the bill.
In order to emphasize the regional character of the new bank, and to ensure that regional and local views are taken into consideration in establishing the policy and operations of the bank, regional advisory councils will be established for each of the five geographic regions of the country. Each council will be composed of up to 12 members from the region, including the two board members, a senior bank officer and a senior officer of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Private members will be appointed by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. These councils, while purely advisory in nature, will assess the bank's activities in their regions and will draw the board of director's attention to the requirements of the small business community in their regions. I believe that these regional advisory councils will serve a useful purpose and will further accent the regional character of the new bank.
The organizational structure of the new bank will be a matter for the board to decide, but it can be envisaged that its corporate structure will be built around two major components, one a financing division and the other, a management services division. These two components will have to be well co-ordinated at different levels of the bank's organization so that a fully client-oriented and comprehensive service is made available to small business in Canada.
While the services of the new bank will be able to build on the experience and organizational structure of the Industrial Development Bank and CASE and other programs which will be brought into it, it will be a big and probably lengthy job to structure a complete service which can meet the requirements of small business in all parts of the country. The government will ensure, however, that those who are put in charge of these services will be qualified to undertake their tasks with initiative and energy.
The financing of the new bank will involve separate budgets for the financial services and for the management services operations. For its financial operations the bank will have an authorized capital of $200 million and a debt-to-equity ratio of ten to one. A capital budget for financing activities will be submitted each year for the approval of the Governor in Council. In accordance with this budget, the Bank will borrow at the Crown corporation rate for the appropriate term. The management services elements of the bank will be financed through parliamentary appropriations in accordance with the normal steps of the budgetary cycle.
The organization which I have outlined will, I think, enable the Federal Business Development Bank to carry out its mandate with a substantial degree of independence. However, its operations will be followed closely by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which, along with other departments, will be represented on the board. It will also be possible for parliament to keep in close touch with the operations of the bank when appro-

priations are considered each year for financing the management services operations.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay tribute to the small businessmen of this country, who, by their initiative, their willingness to take risks and their management of often difficult situations have played an important role in the growth of our national product in the provision of goods and services and in making available substantial employment opportunities. Approximately 60 per cent of the labour force or about five million persons are employed in small business enterprises, broadly defined. Through the Federal Business Development Bank and its other programs the government is showing its support for small businessmen and that it stands ready to help when help is needed.
If such help can enable many small businesses to become medium sized or even big business or at least to become more soundly established and more economically viable, our policies will have shown their worth. If, as well, the Federal Business Development Bank can encourage a substantial number of potential entrepreneurs to enter the field of small business by providing the services they require, the bank will perform, over the years ahead, a very important service to the economy of the country and to the small businessmen who operate a very important part of it. I believe this bill will bring about in a very substantial way the achievement of these important objectives. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, may I urge all parties in this House to support this bill which will provide such important benefits to the nation's small businessmen.

Sometimes it is more meaningful to translate what I have just put in percentage terms into actual terms. In 1963, small business net income in this country was $3.5 billion. In 1973, it was $6.8 billion. It did not even double in that period. On the other hand, let us take a look at corporate profits before taxes in the same period. I remind hon. members that when I say corporate profits before taxes, I am dealing substantially with the nonsmall business sector of the economy. The fact is those profits rose from $4.9 billion in 1963 to $14.8 billion in 1973. As can be seen, they almost tripled in the period this government has ruled Canada whereas small business did not even double its net income in the same period.
As has been pointed out, in recent years, due very heavily to the income tax revisions that this government put into our corporate income tax system, the taxation of corporations has not maintained its relationship to their profitability. Unfortunately, the same tax act has put almost insurmountable difficulties in the way of small businessmen attempting to carry on in the country.
It is an odd government that we have ruling at the present time. I sincerely hope the members of that government will, on this bill at least be given an ample opportunity to stand in their place in this House and give their true feelings concerning the lot of small businessmen in Canada. I say that because I have a certain sympathy for the backbench members in the Liberal party at the present time. speechtext:
Judging from the response of those backbenchers, I have struck a chord and it hurts them deeply.
The bill before us has been described by the minister who introduced it as a great step forward, a mechanism enabling him to do things for small business which have not been done to date. I think we should not accept a statement of that kind without analysis. The fact is that the measure relates in the main to the reconstitution of the Industrial Development Bank. It does contain certain new features, for example, clauses 21, 22 and 23 dealing with management services the bank could offer small businessmen, advisory services to small businessmen and general counselling. But we should not lose sight of the hard fact that the government has always been a friend of big business, and I am fearful it will continue to be so. I say this advisedly, because what we are seeing today is a shifting of the Industrial Development Bank from the Department of Finance to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
We have had some experience of the way in which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has run similar corporations in this country. I am referring, of course, to the Export Development Corporation. The minister has been quite willing to make loans to foreign governments for the benefit of relatively large corporations in Canada, most of them more than 50 per cent foreign-owned. He has been willing to make those loans on a long term basis at interest rates of approximately 7 per cent. Contrast this with the situation today-and I have just checked-in which the current interest rate of the Industrial Development Bank is 11 per cent; for the larger loans it is 12 per cent. The person from whom I obtained this information said it was 12 per cent plus. That is the attitude the

April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank
government takes toward the small businessmen of this country.
There are two annual reports available to us. One is from the Export Development Corporation and the other is from the Industrial Development Bank. Both spell out what it costs to borrow money from the treasury or from the Bank of Canada. The Export Development Corporation points out that loans and advances from the government of Canada totalling 682 million bore interest at rates up to 7% per cent. Dwell on that figure. When we turn to page 22 of the Annual Report of the IDB, we find that loans from the Bank of Canada to the IDB bore an interest rate ranging up to 9Va per cent. In other words, the government is currently lending money to the Export Development Corporation at 7% per cent and to the Industrial Development Bank at 9% per cent. That differential, something over 2 per cent, has to be passed on to the small businessmen. On the other hand, the saving which is represented by the low rate financing on the part of the Export Development Corporation goes indirectly to the benefit of large corporations which, as I have mentioned, are more than 50 per cent foreign-owned.
The needs of businessmen in Canada are simple. First, they need relatively cheap money. They would like to fill out fewer forms for all levels of government. They would like the requirements for collateral in respect of whatever loans they are getting to be reduced. I am not in disagreement with the proposition that they should get advice in management from whoever the new corporation may choose to hire for this purpose. But it is important to realize that the small businessman already knows what his needs are and in most cases there is no point in high-priced Ottawa executives coming down to tell him how to run his business. What he really needs are relatively cheap funds, less government interference in the line of forms to be filled out and a competitive atmosphere in which he can continue and grow.
We should never lose sight of the fact that there is a great difference between big and small business. The socialists to my left often forget this, as do the Liberals from time to time. It is completely wrong to confuse big business with small business. I would think that 90 per cent of the business in this country is carried on by small businessmen who are the backbone of our productivity. I would go further and say that this includes other businessmen such as the farmers who, in truth, are one of the most obvious groups of small businessmen in this country. I would suggest that the small businessman is the great buffer between big business on one corner, big government on another comer and big finance on the third corner of the triangle, if you like.
In my opinion, it is important that the government accept the fact that this is a sector or our economy which requires help and protection, and that this sector at all costs should be preserved. I believe there are five or six points which should be raised as reasons for ensuring that small business continues to prosper and exist in this country. I suggest that a large number of small independent businesses helps preserve competition through ensuring increased efficiency, high quality and reasonable prices for consumers. I suggest also that if we had a truly small

business oriented economy, we would not have the lack of competition and the problems we have today in our country.
If small businesses decrease there is a likelihood that there would be a concentration of excessive economic or political power. Surely, we should always be conscious of the fact that it is just as wrong to have a concentration of economic power as it is to have undue concentration of political power. In my opinion small business constitutes a large and diversified source of employment opportunities. This is something that seems to be overlooked so often by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). Many of his tax measures are designed really to help the larger corporate entity in this country as opposed to the small businessman. In fact small businessmen have mentioned to me that it is extremely difficult for them to live with the current income tax legislation. I am referring to the fact that so many small businessmen find the legislation so confusing that they virtually have to turn over the entire reporting of their income for taxation purposes to their accountants, a service for which they pay substantially higher fees than was the case under the less complicated income tax structure.
I might mention that in the field of new products and new methods, small business is second to none in its innovative stance in ensuring that the country pioneers and develops new fields. I would also suggest that certain things are best done by small business. Small business has the adaptability, resilience and ability to respond to change which bigger companies rarely have. On that point I think it is fair to say that in many cases there is a role for large corporations. Certainly if we expect to become competitive in international markets we need large corporations to meet large corporations. However, I am stressing that this government's passion to help and support big business must be modified so that small business will get a fair share of the national income. I believe personal initiative and individual judgment can be reflected through small business to a much greater extent than is the case in respect of many large corporations, certainly in respect of big government and in respect of being a backbench member of the Liberal Party.
To some extent it has been suggested that small business gives people the opportunity to do in effect their own thing. So many people find frustration in being a relatively insignificant employee, even an executive, in a large corporation that they welcome an opportunity to become active self-employed businessmen in this country. If we agree that small business is an extremely important factor in the economy, I feel we then must analyze the bill before us to determine whether in fact it goes as far as the minister indicates. I suggest it does not. It may be the intent-and I hope in fact it is the intent of the government if it remains in power-to utilize the new corporation to genuinely assist small business, but on the surface I would emphasize again that the bill does not appear to do much more than re-constitute the Industrial Development Bank and give certain other powers to the new corporation.
There are some specific points on which I would like to touch in respect of this new legislation to incorporate this new bank. The minister referred to clause 4 which deals
April 26, 1974

with the corporate objects of the bank. Subclause (2) specifically states:
The Corporation in carrying out its objects shall give particular consideration to the needs of small business enterprises.
I am not sure why subclause (2) is phrased in that manner. I would have thought this bank would give its entire emphasis to supporting small business and not just particular consideration. I say that because if we turn to the annual report of the Bank of Canada we find that in the past year the rate of growth of business loans to small businessmen under authorizations of $100,000 or less was 14 per cent. That is in sharp contrast to the first six months of 1973 when business loans generally went up 23 per cent, and in the last six months of that year went up 31 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue, but if I may I will call it one o'clock and after lunch deal further with specific points in this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to summarize what I was saying before the lunch break. The Liberal government is hostile to small business. There has been a torrent of new laws and regulations, difficult enough for a specialist to understand; interference with small business has increased; extra costs have multiplied for purposes sensible, perhaps, if taken individually, but in the aggregate they are truly excessive; taxes have rocketed for the individual and especially for the individual businessman at a disproportionate rate; incentives have been smothered by the conjunction of a capital gains tax with the present levels of succession duties that still exist in most of our provinces; disclosure requirements have been carried to absurd lengths for small companies; and the rules of the family business or closed company add up to a virtual nightmare for the average businessman in this country. Those rules make his expansion from retained profits virtually impossible.
This Liberal government which has made life so difficult for the small companies has actively encouraged the development of larger corporations, especially those that are foreign controlled. I gave certain figures concerning interest rates where we find that the Industrial Development Bank is lending at rates in excess of 12 per cent to small businessmen in this country, whereas the Export Development Corporation is still facilitating loans to foreign countries to help mainly larger corporations at interest rates which are in the 7 per cent range.
In fact, the country needs businesses of all sizes. Giants make sense in certain world markets-there is no doubt about that. Their production capabilities are needed to compete realistically in the world markets. But I believe that sight should never be lost of the fact that small
Federal Business Development Bank business is an integral part of our economy, certainly as integral as the larger business sector.
I was referring to clause 4 in the bill before us which gives the corporate objects for the new corporation and states, in subclause (2) that it will have particular consideration-that is the new corporation-for the needs of small business enterprise. I find it rather remarkable that no place in this act is there any definition given of a small businessman. I think in fact a small businessman wants to be defined, he wants to understand and to have the government understand what his place is in the economy.
I would also point out to hon. members that no place in the bill is there any suggestion that preferential treatment will be given to Canadian owned concerns as opposed to those that may be controlled in a foreign land. Surely, this could be an integral part of the over-all planning of any government in power. Yet, we find that this government, which at least has given lip service to the idea of some restraint on foreign ownership in Canada, is proposing the incorporation of a new industrial bank, which presumably is completely free, judging from the wording of the act, to lend as much money as they may see fit to Canadian concerns, notwithstanding that they may be foreign controlled. In this respect a former minister of finance in 1963, who at that time was a Liberal member, and I do not mean "Liberal" in today's context as there is no similarity between the Liberal party now and that of 10 or 20 years ago, advanced certain budgetary measures in this House. I refer, of course, to Walter Gordon.
Yesterday in Washington, speaking to the annual meeting of the American Society of International Law, Mr. Gordon indicated that he felt the government's passage of the foreign investment review legislation only covered what he regarded as 20 per cent of the problem in respect of foreign ownership in this country. He stated;
The other 80 per cent of the annual increase in foreign control of Canadian industry is represented by the expansion of foreign controlled companies already established in Canada, companies which often hold a dominant position in their respective industry.
I would tend to agree with Mr. Gordon. Certainly, the legislation passed by this government to date has not had as much effect in restricting or containing foreign ownership in Canada as one would desire. I do find, however, that it is encouraging that Mr. Gordon, in his speech in Washington, has come up with some suggestions for the repatriation of ownership of Canadian concerns now controlled by foreign hands. In fact, in many respects Mr. Gordon's comments are similar to the suggestion contained in the policy papers passed by this party at its recent convention. Most members will recall that at that time we proposed that in the non-renewable resource industry field, at least 50 per cent of equity ownership in these companies should be repatriated into Canadian hands.
I mention this because I feel that so much of what the Liberal government does, it does in an ad hoc fashion. It passes one act which is supposed to restrain foreign ownership expansion in this country and yet, apparently with no inter-relationship whatsoever, it has its Crown corporations actively supporting foreign corporations in the land,

April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank or is passing new acts which in all likelihood will benefit some foreign corporations presently active in the country.
In introducing the bill the Acting Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) indicated how well he felt the government had done in respect of small businesses. He perhaps did not realize at the time he was speaking that the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen was at that moment suing the Canadian government for almost $100 million. That association, on behalf of 13,000 members, feels that it has a claim against the federal government as a result of its haphazard handling of the post office dispute. What an odd twist in that here we have a government introducing a bill which it professes to be in the best interests of small businessmen in the country, who it indicates it has been supporting, yet we have a 13,000 member federation of independent small businessmen at the same time suing the same government for $100 million as a result of its mismanagement of the post office strike.
If I may deal with other aspects of this bill, I should like to touch on provisions 21, 22 and 23 which deal with management consulting, management training and the provision of information and advice to small business people. We believe this is probably a good step as we think such consulting, advice and information should be given by the federal government to small business. We do question, however, and if this bill reaches committee we intend to question this further, whether it is necessary to have this type of service within the bank itself. We question whether the responsibility of the bank in lending money, and in ensuring its return, will blend well with the counselling and advisory services such as contemplated in these clauses.
I would point out in this regard that in the United States, in the United Kingdom and in certain other of the western industrialized nations there has been a tendency to set up separate bureaux to help small businessmen in the same way as is contemplated in the three clauses. It may be that the divorcing of that advisory type of function from the banking function is a wise move. We are in agreement with the provision of that service, but we should like to know why it is being included within the banking function itself.
I believe we, as members, should not accept the suggestion that the chartered banks in Canada do not wish to lend money to small businesses. In all fairness, this is a business proposition as far as our chartered banks are concerned. The banks must determine whether they can make advantageous loans, properly secured to ensure the return of capital at a fair rate of return. It is only common sense to realize that it is much easier to make a million dollar loan, a loan of $10 million or even $100 million to a credit worthy company at a relatively good interest rate, and to make a worth-while return, than it is to make loans of $25,000 with all the added work and possible security risk.
I would emphasize that fact when I say there must be assistance to small businesses. I feel we are simply being realistic in respect of how the marketplace works, and that is why it is right and proper that institutions such as the Industrial Development Bank and, hopefully, the new Federal Business Development Bank, if and when it is

incorporated, will be active in that field. I would point out, and this should not be lost sight of, that this is a field which has already been entered to some extent by provincial governments. Many of our provinces are quite active in the field of supporting small businesses. If you review the annual report of the Industrial Development Bank you may be as surprised as I was that one-third of the volume of its lending in the fiscal year 1973 was in British Columbia, involving 2,835 loans totalling some $124 million odd. I asked the Industrial Development Bank why that was so. They pointed out that British Columbia is one of the few provinces that does not have a provincial agency financing activities of small business. Consequently, the IDB has a bigger role to play in that province that in most other provinces.
The second reason they gave for their activity in British Columbia was the fact that more than most provinces, it has many frontier type businesses in operation which find their type of loan quite attractive. I am pleased that the IDB has been taking that type of lead, and I hope that the new Federal Business Development Bank will take a similar lead in support of small businesses if and when it is incorporated.
I would draw the attention of hon. members to clause 36 which deals with voting, or not voting, by directors if loans involving them are being considered by the board of the new corporation. It came as a surprise to me that it would even have been contemplated by the federal government that future directors of the new bank would be able to borrow from it. Granted, the clause requires that:
A director shall not vote on a resolution relating to, or be present at a meeting of the board during the time at the meeting when the board is considering, a loan to, a guarantee to, a guarantee of a loan to, an underwriting agreement with, or a purchase from, that director or a firm or corporation of which
(a) that director,...
is a partner or shareholder, as the case may be.
If this bill reaches committee I think it should be explained, bearing in mind that there are only ten outside directors on this board, why it is felt necessary to have any one of those directors eligible for a loan directly or indirectly, from this bank.
Now, I should like to deal with clause 36 dealing with the appointment of an auditor. This is quite unlike the present Industrial Development Bank provision. The proposal is that there be only one auditor in future, although the Industrial Development Bank has two auditors. I think this should be explained. It should also be explained why it is proposed to appoint the auditor for five years instead of a more limited term.
I have reviewed what I believe to be some of the main provisions that should be considered in this act, and have tried to indicate why I feel that small businessmen deserve assistance as well as encouragement from any federal government. In addition, I have indicated why I believe this federal government has not given such assistance or encouragement to them, nor to the country, and also why in many instances they are openly hostile to small businesses.
April 26, 1974

Just before we recessed for lunch the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that he found it interesting that I somehow linked his party with the Liberal Party, pointing out as he did that I, on the one hand, talked socialism and then suggested that the Liberal Party was quite close to big business. I would refer him to the comments of John Kenneth Galbraith, a sometime Canadian who said we must bear in mind that:
In North American society, the big business bureaucracy and the public bureaucracy work in close alliance and the goals of this alliance are essentially in conflict with the interest of most individual members of North American society. There is a system of several thousand giant corporations which dominate the economic life of the continent. The bureaucracy of this corporate world in alliance with the public bureaucracy is increasingly the focus of public power and is responsible for the inequities and irrationalities which are deeply inherent in the structure of the system in all developed countries.
I mention that because I feel that Galbraith is referring to the fact that there are the two extremes. You have big business, big bureaucracy and big money and in between you have this great mass of small businessmen and small farmers who are really the backbone of the productive capacity of any country. Any government that allows that central group of independent business people to be trampled by government or big business, is not a good government. That is why I feel it is so urgent that we, as members, make this our concern. I sincerely hope that the backbench members of the Liberal Party, on this bill at least, will have the courage to say what they think concerning the lot of the small businessman in this country in the last ten years under their rule.
Mr. Speaker, I know that we have people on this side of the House who wish to speak on this bill. I will conclude by saying that we are thankful for anything that appears to be helpful to small businessmen. We do not intend to vote against this bill on second reading. We hope that if it is as helpful as the minister has indicated, it will be well received by small businessmen. We feel that the bill should have good and extensive debate, that it should go to committee to be thoroughly reviewed and perhaps amended, then returned to this House in relatively short order for third reading.

speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker, now that I have had time for lunch I have recovered, and hopefully will be able to continue.
It would be interesting to tabulate the number of times the minister mentioned small business during that presentation, which emphasizes the point I have previously made. I remember that he mentioned small business many, many times. Actually, I ran for election to this House because I wanted to fight for better legislation for that important sector of society, small business. The government has recognized how important that segment is. I shall not go into more detail, as it may appear I am criticizing the Industrial Development Bank. At this point may I commend my own local bank office for the co-operation and encouragement it has extended over the years. Unfortunately it was restricted by the guidelines laid down in the act.
May I mention areas of concern to small business. Small businesses play an important role in the Canadian economy, creating over 50 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product, paying 50 per cent of taxes collected by government-an important consideration to bear in mind if the government is to continue spending more and more money-and employing more than 50 per cent of the people working in Canada.
There are at least eight important economic functions performed by small businesses. For instance, small businesses provide a productive outlet for the energies of that large group of enterprising and independent people who attach great value to economic independence. Many of these people are less suited to employment in a large organization but have much to contribute to the over-all vitality of the economy. Often, a small business is the most efficient form of business organization. That is why many important trades and industries are made up mainly of small businesses. Many small businesses act as specialist suppliers to large companies of parts, sub-assemblies or components which can be produced at a cost lower than that which can be achieved by large companies. In addition, small businesses add greatly to the variety of products and services offered to the consumer, because they can flourish in a limited or specialized market which it would not be worth the while of a larger business to enter.
In an economy in which ever larger multi-product businesses are emerging, small businesses provide competition, actual and potential, and provide some check on monopoly profits and the inefficiency which monopoly breeds. In this way they contribute to the efficient working of the economic system as a whole.
Despite their relatively lower expenditures on research and development, small businesses are an important source of innovation in products, techniques and services. May I refer to my own case. With the co-operation of employees, we brought forward new products. I am thinking of two cases in which we evolved equipment for which we took out Canadian and U.S. patents. I suggest that a bigger business would not have done this, as the sort of
1802_______________________COMMONS DEBATES__________________ April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank
equipment we make is sold in small quantities. It would not have been developed if we were not a small business.
Further, Mr. Speaker, the small business sector is the traditional embryo or breeding ground for new industries. What is most important, small businesses provide the means of entry into business for new entrepreneurial talent and the seed bed from which new, large companies will grow to challenge and stimulate the established leaders of industry. Despite its important economic role, the small business in Canada is weakening because it finds it increasingly difficult to cope with the many problems confronting it.
One of the major difficulties confronting small business today is the difficulty of obtaining funds. Fundamentally, the problem may be summarized this way: owing to their limited economic base, small businesses find it difficult to raise funds on the capital market and have had to turn either to self-financing or bank credit. In many cases self-financing involves difficulties owing to the limited profit margins. As far as bank credit is concerned, small businesses suffer from certain handicaps as compared with the big firms. In the first place they cannot offer the same security and, second, the smallness of their loans involves the banks in higher administrative costs. The small businesses are therefore less attractive customers to banks than the big firms and this fact has its repercussions on the terms they can obtain. Third, the volume of investment loans to the smaller enterprises is apt to fluctuate because financial institutions have a tendency to start by cutting their money supply to the smaller enterprises when the money market becomes tight and to increase it when the money market becomes easier.
While the most obvious source of capital is the venture capital firm, entrepreneurs are reluctant to use this source for the following reasons: first, venture capital firms tend to want to assume equity control of the firm in which they invest; second, venture capital firms insist on appointing their own company executives on the Board of Directors of the firm, and may go so far as to wrest complete control from the entrepreneur by having their own man assume the responsibility of chief executive officer; third, venture capital firms which have acquired effective control of the entrepreneur's company tend to prevent the entrepreneur from acquiring additional capital through equity participation for fear of weakening their control. The preoccupation with the issue of control appears to be the critical factor underlying the resistance of entrepreneurs against utilizing the services of venture capital groups.
Governments in many industrialized countries have found it necessary or desirable to make special provision for privileged access by small businesses to external finance. The measures taken for this purpose most commonly take the following forms: first, the establishment of specialist institutions-with access to loans or grants from government sources-which are able to co-operate with, and support, commercial banks in their lending operations; second, the provision of rediscount facilities to commercial banks by official institutions, including, ultimately, the central bank, for at least a proportion of their term loans; third; official financial support and encouragement for the establishment, by commercial banks of affiliated financial institutions specializing in term loans to small

and medium-sized concerns; fourth, official financial support and encouragement for the formation of trade associations and co-operatives which make term loans available to their members; fifth, the establishment of, or financial support for, institutions and co-operatives which guarantee the credit standing of small businesses seeking term finance; sixth, subsidization of interest rates charged by institutions lending to small businesses.
The best known of such policies are those of the United States where the Small Business Administration, an administrative body set up specifically for small businesses, has been empowered to subsidize loans to small business, that is to say, the interest rate on loans to small businesses is subsidized.
May I mention two or three other areas which involve concern and frustration for the small businessman. For example, the numerous bureaucratic government forms which the small businessman must fill out when applying for a loan add to his confusion and difficulty. In addition, the large collateral demanded by the Industrial Development Bank makes it difficult for a small businessman to get a loan. The chartered banks have not been sympathetic in their administration of small business loans. I hope lending institutions will adopt a different attitude under this legislation. In any event, the government should adopt a Canada first policy when considering loans to businesses. I suggest that loans could be based on the percentage of Canadian equity in the company. The existing legislation has tended to favour foreign subsidiaires getting loans, simply because they can provide more collateral for loans than Canadian companies can. I suggest that we should favour giving priority to Canadian businesses seeking loans.
As the previous speaker suggested, a small business should be more clearly defined in the bill. The volume of lending assistance should be subject to parliamentary approval, as well. The bank to be set up should be more flexible in its attitude to collateral requirements. The requirement for collateral should be calculated on an overall, average basis, rather than for each individual loan. As I said previously and as my party has also pointed out, it has been almost impossible for the small businessman of this country to gain access to capital. The idea is this, if you put a maximum of $5,000 each year into a small business, a small business being defined as a company having a net worth of up to $1 million and annual revenue up to $10 million, you will be able to claim a tax credit in chat year of $2,500. You can apply this $2,500 against your income tax or have it rebated to you directly.
The advantage of the tax credit will remain with you so long as you continue to hold the investment, but will be repayable to the government if and when the investment is realized. If you do not recover your investment, the amount of credit repayable will be half of your recovery. If you realize a gain, the gain will be taxable in the ordinary way and there will be no capital loss deduction allowed.
Regardless of how this bill may look to small businessmen, I question whether it will go as far as he really needs. As I emphasized in the remarks I made on Bill C-14,

the small business and farm improvements act, the most significant void in that bill was the lack of working capital available. I am sure this bill will pass all stages. I trust when that is done it will be of some benefit and encouragement to an area which is very close to me and for which, as long as I am here, I intend to stand up and fight.

Mr. Speaker, the bill we are discussing today is little more than a renaming of the act which established the Industrial Development Bank. The reason we are changing the name of the act and expanding the programs this bank will be able to deal with is that in this country we tend to deal in a very fragmented way with social-economic groups which need assistance.
We have given the banks, insurance companies and trust companies the virtually unlimited right to decide how to dispense the savings of the people of Canada which are deposited with them for re-investment. With regard to the needs of those who want to borrow money, this is not done on the basis of social need, but on the basis of what is most profitable for the banks, insurance companies and trust companies. In that kind of situation, it is not surprising that the bulk of the money which the banks, insurance companies and trust companies lend goes to the largest and most profitable corporations in this country many of which, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out, are in fact multi-national corporations. Money is loaned to those foreign-owned and controlled corporations by the lending organizations such as banks, trust companies and mortgage companies. They are not concerned about the social return to the people who are asking the individuals or organizations for loans.
They do not deal with the kind of people and organizations which are forced to go to the Industrial Development Bank and, after this bill is passed, will be going to the new banking corporation which will be set up. That means very often those things which are most needed in this country are not available. We do not receive the amount of money that should be put into housing, particularly housing for people with moderate or low incomes. Rather, a decision has been made to funnel money into office buildings which very often are not needed. No wonder the small businessmen suffer compared to the large corporations.
I was interested in hearing the hon. member for York-Simcoe point out that profits of large corporations before taxes almost tripled in the past 10 years, increasing from $4 billion to over $14 billion. It was because we in the New Democratic Party knew this kind of situation was developing and accelerating that we were so active in supporting the recommendations of the Carter royal commission which was appointed by the former Conservative government under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) to look into the problems of taxation.
The Carter commission recommended that our tax system should be based on the simple principle that a dollar of income, regardless of whether it is earned in the form of wages, salaries, interest, real estate speculation or stock dividends, is a dollar that should be taxed in the same way. I remind the hon. member for York-Simcoe, who was not here at that time, that his party was very
Federal Business Development Bank hostile toward those kinds of recommendations. They thought then, and as far as I know still do, that that kind of tax policy was bad. They basically supported the kind of tax policy we have had in this country for many years under both Liberal and Conservative governments whereby special consideration and concessions are traditionally given to big business, particularly the kind of concessions which have and care being given to the resource industries, the largest and most foreign dominated companies in this country.
