record. When that proposal was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) it was supported by the Official Opposition. The hon. member for York-Simcoe was complaining that big industry had done well by comparison with small business. I suggest that if the large corporations paid a fair share of taxation, working men, farmers and small businessmen would do a hell of a lot better. If the government would adopt the principle that it has a duty and a right to take part in the planning required to meet the needs of the country, the kind of bill which is now before us would be superfluous.
The government already asks the banks to do certain things. It already tells the chartered banks they must maintain a certain level of reserves in relation to the amount they lend. We say the government should accept its responsibility for planning to meet the needs of the country and do so in part by directing the banks, the trust companies and other financial institutions as to the particular fields to which capital should be allotted. In other words, the banks, mortgage companies and the insurance companies should be required to direct a portion of their available money to housing instead of office buildings, to farms instead of gasoline stations and to small businessmen rather than giant supermarket chainstores.
In this way the lending institutions would use their resources-money which, in any case, is not theirs, but belongs to the people of Canada,-not merely to the advantage of the banks and mortgage companies, so that more profit would be gained, but in such a way that the basic needs of the people could be met. If this were government policy, the ad hoc approach inherent in the kind of bill before us would not be necessary, because money would be available through existing institutions. However, this is not the policy of Liberal governments, nor of Conservative governments. I am not surprised they are not prepared to accept this concept. As a result though, we find ourselves dealing with the kind of proposals which are before us today, and in the absence of anything better we shall support this idea with respect to change from Industrial Development Bank to Federal Business Development Bank.
However, I am a member of parliament from a have-not province and I must take into account the needs of the people of my province, my area and my city-the needs of all people, with no account taken of political differences or differences between cities and rural areas. The four western provinces, three of them-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia-with NDP governments and the Province of Alberta, with a Conservative government, met in Calgary in July of 1973, almost a year ago. They discussed a number of subjects and reached agreement on a number of subjects-surprisingly, I suppose, in the light of the differing complexions of those governments. One of three subjects was capital financing and financial institutions. They were critical of the Industrial Development Bank and the manner in which it has functioned until now.
I want to spend a few moments putting on record the substance of this criticism, with which, essentially, I agree. The provinces made a number of suggestions which I commend to the minister and which I hope the new bank will keep in mind when it begins its operations, so that it

will work better than the IDB did. Let me quote a few sections from the statement made by the four western premiers.
The Western Provinces find the Industrial Development Bank deficient in several respects. To increase the effectiveness of the Bank as a vehicle for stimulating economic development in the Western Provinces in particular and the rest of Canada in general, the Western Provinces recommend that the Industrial Development Bank:
(1)	provide substantially greater assistance than in the past to
higher-risk ventures;
(2)	explore the possibility of taking equity positions in existing
firms and of establishing new companies based on joint private and
public ownership; and
(3)	broaden the types of services which it offers to small business.
They went on in some detail to explain what they meant
when they listed the objectives I have already placed on the record. They say that small and medium sized businesses are of crucial importance to the economy of western Canada. They state that firms earning less than $100,000 of taxable income per annum comprise over 80 per cent of the total companies in both western and central Canada. These relatively small firms in western Canada contribute a larger portion of the total taxation income than do similar firms in central Canada.
Anybody who has visited western Canada or the northern part of Canada knows how important the branch bank, the local department store, the drug store and the clothing store are to the community and how the closing of one such store can lead to the virtual extinction of a small town or village. It is for that reason the premiers urged that the stimulation of the growth and expansion of small enterprise be given major priority at all levels of government. The Industrial Development Bank was supposed to be a major federal agency to provide assistance to small business. Since its establishment in 1944 its primary function supposedly has been to provide capital assistance to industry with particular consideration being given to the financing problems of small enterprises.
However, frequently it has been difficult, if not impossible, for many small companies to obtain assistance from the Industrial Development Bank. Before 1961 financial aid was offered only to firms in the manufacturing sector. Since then an amendment was made to the Industrial Development Bank Act and the bank was able to move into other fields, but the loans have been relatively small. Half the loans have been in amounts of $25,000 or less and 80 per cent of the loans have been for amounts of $50,000 or less. The bank has assisted in the development of many small scale enterprises but its participation has been limited for a number of reasons.
The Royal Commission on Banking and Finance and the Gray Report noted that the Industrial Development Bank's lending policies have tended to be too conservative. They pointed out that the bank's loan ratio has been only approximately 0.5 per cent of annual disbursements. This suggests that the bank has not been involved in very many high risk ventures. When the bank takes that attitude it means the lending of money for high risk ventures is left almost exclusively to provincial development corporations.
April 26, 1974

It is for this reason that the record of those provincial development agencies in every province has been pretty bad. They have had to take the risk of lending money to those companies which could not obtain the money from the commercial banks, insurance companies or trust companies or from the Industrial Development Bank. The western premiers therefore suggest that this bank be prepared to take more risks than it has so that the needs of small business, more particularly in the western provinces and in the maritime provinces, can be met. They point out that the Industrial Development Bank's assistance to small business has also been severely limited because of this reluctance to enter into joint ventures with privately owned firms. The Industrial Development Bank Act authorizes the bank to take an equity position, but the bank has not used that authority. The distribution of loans among the provinces is another matter which gives the western premiers a great deal of concern.
If one looks at the accumulative record of the Industrial Development Bank it is obvious that the bulk of the loans have gone to the central provinces which are now the most prosperous. From 1944 until September 30, 1972, 30.2 per cent of all the loan money which the bank authorized went to the province of Ontario while 23.9 per cent of the money loaned by the Industrial Development Bank went to the province of Quebec. Companies in the province of British Columbia received 21 per cent of the money loaned by the Industrial Development Bank. When one looks at the situation in respect of the other provinces one realizes how restrictive the Industrial Development Bank has been until now. The province of Nova Scotia received 2.2 per cent of the money. The province of New Brunswick received 2.4 per cent of the money. The province of Manitoba received 4.6 per cent of the money. The province of Saskatchewan received 3.3 per cent of the money, and the province of Alberta received 9.3 per cent of the money. That performance is not good enough if the bank is to be of any assistance to the existing commercial banks and mortgage and trust companies.
Surely this federal government bank ought to have some social purposes. One of its main functions should be to meet the needs of the have-not provinces. I say, as the premiers have said much more effectively, that the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have obtained collectively 17.2 per cent of the value of all the loans granted by the Industrial Development Bank. The Atlantic provinces have acquired only 6.6 per cent of the money authorized for loans by the bank. This simply is not good enough. I say to the minister that the new bank with its new board, and with the regional advisory committee which the minister outlined when he introduced this bill, simply must be instructed not about whether to give a particular loan but to pay a good deal more attention to the needs and requirements of the have-not provinces of Canada, whether they be on the Atlantic coast or in the prairie region.
The four premiers made, in the submission which they published in July of 1973, three recommendations. I think that they should be put on the record and that the government should give serious consideration to adopting them. First, they recommended that the bank provide substan-
Federal Business Development Bank tially greater assistance than in the past to high risk ventures. Instead of restricting assistance only to enterprises which possess a substantial amount of collateral, the bank should also assist those businesses which may not have an abundance of collateral but which present sound business proposals.
Second, the bank should explore the possibility of taking equity positions in existing firms and of establishing new companies based on joint private and public ownership. This would help to fill the gap for ventured capital which currently exists in Canada.
Third, it is recommended that the bank broaden the type of services which it offers to small businesses. It should desist from relying almost exclusively on the provision of loan capital and should provide other services, such as consultative services to management, technical assistance in the securing of contracts, etc.
I will close by quoting from the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance as follows:
The aim of government institutions should not be to get the maximum number of loans on their books. Rather it should be to ensure that businesses which can be competitive and profitable have access on a reasonable basis both to a variety of sources of funds and to guidance in planning their financial affairs.
The recommendation of the Western Economic Opportunities Conference was as follows:
... the Industrial Development Bank should provide a substantially greater amount of financial assistance to such regions as the prairie provinces and the Atlantic provinces. In so doing, it would bring about a more equitable participation by all regions of Canada in industrial activities.
That statement came from the four premiers of western Canada representing two different political parties, but I am certain that if there had been a Liberal premier in one of those provinces, he would have endorsed the statements made by the present four premiers.

this country than the Industrial Development Bank has been until now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words about the establishment of the new bank.
We are, Mr. Speaker, partly satisfied with the introduction of that bill because we feel that we already have an organization which could perform that work. The Industrial Development Bank with its branches in every area of the country could surely serve the population. If new responsibilities were given to the Industrial Development Bank, we could, Mr. Speaker, save up in administration costs.
The administration could be less costly, but since we are setting up a new bank, it will require a new staff and consequently the administration will cost millions of dollars in public funds.
Instead of providing benefits to the small industry under the present system, we will probably be compelled to lend money at very high rates so that the small industry will not directly profit by the legislation or that bank which could give cheap credit to produce cheaply.
The purpose of the new organizations which we are setting up such as the proposed one, should be to encourage Canadians to produce or to develop further the small or medium Canadian industries to have them produce cheaply.
For them to be able to produce cheaply, interest rates would necessarily have to be brought down to a decent level, let us say no higher than 3 per cent, so we could really produce at a lower cost.
Interest rates, Mr. Speaker, are the prime factor in the increase in prices and the cost of living. Interest rates are primarily responsible for any increase in the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, a new institution of economic development such as the one provided for in this bill might help big business, but what about the small business? They always claim to promote small and medium-sized businesses when actually, with all the existing old institutions, big business has always been favoured. Small businesses have always found it difficult to take advantage of regulations and legislation to avail themselves directly of the benefits offered by those institutions.

The benefits are for big industries that borrow millions and millions of dollars because they are fortunate enough to have capital stock or to sell shares in their operation, while small businesses are far from having the same possibilities. It is easier for big businesses with capital stock to operate and produce with their capital stocks than with borrowed capital, because industry must pay back borrowed capital with interest. Small businesses never have working capital while a business with capital stock does not have to make payments, pay back interest and, therefore, that industry has more working capital with which to operate. It seems to me that this should be included in this bill in order to help small business. We could also help him by establishing lower interest rates.
If the government is able to guarantee loans to the industry, then they should also be able to guarantee reasonable interest rates. There is no reference to interest rate but I know it will be the same as that charged by other institutions and it is presently too high; it is therefore nearly useless to try to produce.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, both small businessmen and big industry are forced to operate on a seasonal basis. Some products become seasonal; they must be stored for five, six, seven or even eight months, and storage is very expensive. The industrialist, who is unable to support storage charges, is again forced to borrow money from chartered banks, under what is known as the 88 formula, and interest rates are presently 12 per cent. Thus, when the storage of some products for several months must be financed at high interest rates, the interest gulps the benefits of the small business.
In this bill, we should provide for financing storage at a very low interest rate to allow small businesses to operate normally. We could allow them to have a working capital and to manufacture more cheaply. Also, the small businesses often have another problem that the medium and large industries do not have, that of transportation. Indeed, it is a well-known fact that in general small businesses are located far from the major centres, do not have suitable highways or throughways, and must therefore pay excessive transportation rates which eat up part of their profits.
Here again, the government should do something to help the small businesses to organize since they cannot pay the excessive transportation rates. They should be able to operate their business and transport their goods in time and more economically, which would allow them to develop more rapidly. For this reason, they should have access to the Industrial Development Bank, which could provide more capital at more reasonable interest rates so that small businesses could operate more economically. Several small industries cannot operate if they do not have their own transportation system and transport goods directly to their destination.
Mr. Speaker, we should also be able to provide the small businesses with reasonable income tax rates. I know that this cannot be included in this Bill, but it should be provided for the small business, for instance those with a turnover of less than $1 million should benefit from a tax exemption, because with a turnover of $50,000, $100,000, or $1 million, small industry cannot assume all those costs without some form of assistance. Small industry is over-
April 26, 1974

taxed and income taxes are excessive. There should also be provision, in addition to reasonable income tax rates, for a certain deductible turnover. Furthermore, small industry should be non-taxable if its turnover is less than $1 million.
Then, Mr. Speaker, it would be of great benefit to the small industry to consider each individual sector and introduce a bill which would really help small and medium industries in general, for the large industry has no problem.
Major industries, which can be listed on the stock market have no problems, but those unable to do so have all kinds of problems: labour, taxes, and so on. It is very difficult for the small industry to survive and even flourish because it has to pay in all sectors, for all administrative services, federal and provincial, municipal and school. School boards and municipalities take unfair advantage of small industry, depriving it of all its working capital.
Mr. Speaker, we know that the government's job is to manage, therefore, we should give it the opportunity to do so, since it can and because now the opposition also has a say in the matter.
A few minutes ago, I listened to an hon. member from the New Democratic Party who made suggestions and offered solutions. Some Progressive Conservative members did the same. At this time we have a government which is listening to the suggestions made by the opposition. Therefore, I believe we now have one of the best governments we ever had in Canada, because the opposition really has the opportunity to make its contribution. Moreover, the views of the opposition are to a large degree taken into consideration. That is why I say we have one of the best governments ever.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government collects a tax of 12 per cent on anything produced made in Canada. In view of the almost overall increase in the cost of living at a rate of 25 to 30 per cent, it would seem reasonable I think for the government to consider the lowering of that 12 per cent tax. This 12 per cent excise tax should at least be reduced, Mr. Speaker, and if the minister was willing to consider our suggestion, we would be very happy.
It is generally known that a higher cost of living generally increases government's income, and that the 12 per cent excise tax brings in far more to the government. Now, if it were reduced, all Canadians would benefit from it, and this would contribute most certainly to reducing the cost of living and the cost of goods. I am of the opinion that this suggestion should be considered by the minister.
This new institution should then be adapted to new techniques on the basis of facts and of today's realities and not of past traditions. If this new institution is set up according to old customs, we will only get the same results as in the past.
I ask the minister to consider the situation. Even if we can move amendments, I feel we should leave this task to the minister. It should suffice to ask him to do so. He could change the bill himself, with a view to really granting the required advantages to small and medium industries,
Federal Business Development Bank because if we really want to develop a strong country, our industries and institutions must also be strong.
Every day a number of small industries have to close down because they cannot stay in business, while it is those industries which support the big ones. Large industries extract the raw materials that are consumed and processed by the small and medium-sized industries.
That completes the industrial and economic cycle because large industries cannot produce at a lower cost than small industries. The latter are often family businesses where people work 10, 15 and even 18 hours a day. They work almost night and day and working hours mean nothing. That is why the small industry can produce at a lower cost than the big industry which must close at fixed hours and operate only 48 hours a week. Then it has to close because employees will not work any longer because the law prevents them or because they must be paid double time. In small family industries, people work as they like and, as long as they like, they produce at a lower cost and technical management, bookkeeping, accounting all that is done in the evening. During the day, many owners work as employees and at night, even on Sunday sometimes, they look after their accounting in the spare time.
That is why one can infer that small industries produce at a lower cost than big industries. Therefore, we should encourage the small business which is the backbone of our society and to a great extent the basis of all other businesses. Big industrial producers depend upon it, because it processes a good deal of their raw materials or products. It markets those finished products at a much lower cost.
This is one of the reasons why we will support this bill, but we are not really enthusiastic because we think that it will not meet our present economic needs. It will not give to small businessmen what they are entitled to expect from their government.
Mr. Speaker, this government is here to get results, to guarantee production means to small businessmen. Guaranteeing production means in the small industry is only a matter of financing. Today it is difficult to get loans at a small interest rate and even at higher rates. Many small businessmen cannot get any loan because our financial institutions say they are not solvent enough, that they already owe too much and should not run deeper into debt. Then, Mr. Speaker, several industries are now at a standstill because they already got a small loan of $25,000, $35,000 or $50,000. They wish to expand and buy new equipment. However they are unable to get one more penny on the market because they cannot get a new loan from those who did lend them money on a first mortgage unless those industries increase and even double their production. To double their production, they need twice as much money and they cannot find it anywhere. Then they are stopped because they lack funds that should be at their disposal.
I think that everything which is physically possible should financially be so. The government should assume its responsibility and lend money at reasonable interest rates to check the increase, in the cost of living.
Nowadays, large financial institutions make billions of dollars in profit, as do the banks for that matter. All ten

April 26, 1974
Federal Business Development Bank Canadian chartered banks increased their assets by about fifteen billion dollars in 1973.
Mr. Speaker, if such increases in assets do not pass all bounds, then I do not know what does. With an assets increase of 228 per cent, those institutions could make a little less profit and give more money to the people to live on.
The government, out of honesty, clear-mindedness and initiative, must ask those institutions to be reasonable, and if they refuse, we can, through our banks or other institutions such as the one we are creating now, be reasonable and not only charge the same interest rates as they do, like the Industrial Development Bank, for instance, which keeps pace with other institutions. If the others raise their interest rates, the Industrial Development Bank does the same much before the others. It is always ahead of the others in that respect because it charges a higher interest than the other institutions.
Therefore, it is not an institution which helps people but one which exploits them and allows the other institutions to survive and exploit the population.
Mr. Speaker, we are against that type of exploitation and against financial organizations, which should be there to help rather than to exploit the people.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR INCORPORATION, OBJECTS, REGIONAL ADVISORY COUNCILS, POWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in this debate I am reminded of the story of two small businessmen who met at a social gathering. One said to the other, "How's business?" The reply was, "Well, I didn't make enough money to retire last year and I didn't lose enough to go bankrupt.' I believe that typifies the condition of most small business people today. A recent statistic produced by the Bank of Canada shows that the share of national income going to smaller business has declined by a full three percentage points. In 1962 the share of national income going to small business was 19.5 per cent. In 1973 that share had eroded to 7.5 per cent. The decline has been gradual year by year and shows there is a long standing and serious difficulty in the field of small business
In one sense I welcome this bill, for it calls for the restructuring of the Industrial Development Bank into a new Federal Business Development Bank. I welcome it in one sense because, on the surface, it may be a partial answer to the difficulties facing small business. We need to take a comprehensive look at the entire picture. That is, we must examine the financing needs of small business, look at managerial and marketing skills and examine taxation applying to small businesses.
Attention must also be paid to the growing demands of Statistics Canada on small businesses. I should like the minister to take the initiative in this matter. I ask him to obtain from Statistics Canada one copy of all forms which Statistics Canada sends to small businesses. These forms could be presented to the Standing Committee on Industry, Trade and Commerce. We could ask Statistics Canada officials to appear before the standing committee and prove the necessity of these forms and questionnaires. I should like to see current procedures changed. Let new forms be cleared by the standing committee and let us allow spokesmen from small businessmen's organizations

to provide some input to the standing committee in this matter. The average small businessman just does not have the time or staff to climb the paper work mountain which is facing him today.
A constituent of mine wrote to me about this. I shall read part of his letter, as follows:
Enclosed is a copy of a letter to Statistics Canada. I find it extremely difficult to understand why at least once a month for the last many months we have had to waste time filling out this type of form. I run a one girl office, have done for ten years, and do not plan to change this, and can certainly not see any reason for the extreme waste of taxpayers money in this sort of ridiculous questionaire. Surely it is time that some of these obvious make programs should be looked into.
Many small businessmen have expressed the same views to me. The author of the letter is a doctor with a small practice in Burlington. His inquiry is typical of many similar ones which have come to me from the small business community.
It is somewhat ironic that the Industrial Development Bank was created some 30 years ago to be a lender of last resort, especially for small enterprises. Now it is being restructured, to be known as the Federal Business Development Bank which is being set up to help small enterprises especially.
The obvious question is, what has happened in the intervening 30 years? Is not the IDB doing the job it is supposed to do for small business? If you want the answers, you need only talk to people who have used the services of IDB. I wonder if we are only changing the name, adding the counselling and consultative service, removing the IDB from the shadow of the Bank of Canada and placing it totally under the authority of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Gillespie). That is a good move and I support that part of the bill.
In many cases what happens is this. When the small businessman goes to the local bank manager and asks for a loan, the bank manager actually suggests that he should go to the Industrial Development Bank. When you come to that stage you have passed step one in the loan process; you have been refused a loan by your local bank manager. The IDB manager and your local bank manager put their heads together and talk over the phone, at which time your account is discussed and the bank rate revealed. At this point the IDB is in the driver's seat. You need money to carry on your project and your bank has turned you down. Then IDB sends one of its loan officers and engineers to see you. After discussion, he usually indicates whether or not he feels you may be granted a loan. The interest rate is then discussed.
The Industrial Development Bank has been accused of lending money at rates lower than those charged in the private sector and of competing openly with the private sector. I have read these accusations but have not seen such cases. The IDB has been accused of competing openly with the private sector and undercutting rates. As the bank pays no income tax, its actions have been classed as unfair competition. I should like to see evidence of this. I have read in various places that the bank does this. My experience is completely the opposite. I have found IDB rates to be between IV2 and 2 per cent above the rate available to small businessmen.
April 26, 1974

What really ties the small businessman down is the security IDB takes. It will be interesting to see if the new Federal Business Development Bank will follow the same procedures. I have found that IDB insists on a debenture on all the company's assets, a charge on fixed assets, insurance policies on the life of the president or owner, a claim on receivables and inventory, and a secondary position with relation to the commercial bank, where those assets are used as collateral with the commercial bank. You will find, as well, that IDB will usually take collateral mortgages on the owner's residence as well as personal guarantees by the owner or president of the company and the directors of the company. This massive collateral acts like a millstone round the neck of the entrepreneurial ability of the small businessman. It tends to negate the basic philosophy behind limited companies, that of shielding shareholders from personal liability.
The danger, as I see it, is that the Federal Business Development Bank may be only a cosmetic change. We may be seeing merely a change of name and the addition of a few consultative services. Clearly we need new people at the top and a totally new philosophy for stressing the entrepreneurial aspect of business. We need people who will seize on the innovative abilities of small businessmen and be more of a partner to assist and guide the small businessman. That is the attitude we need, rather than the heavy handed attitude of collateral security.
I do not see why the new bank should not take preferred stock in a small company as collateral, instead of debentures, floating charges and personal guarantees. I would much rather see the Federal Business Development Bank shake itself loose from the traditional bank approach and take a leaf from the book of, say, the Toronto-Dominion Bank. That bank went outside the circle of bank employees and employed people from business to head its Toronto-Dominion venture capital group.
Because of the failure of IDB to answer the needs of small business, we have witnessed the proliferation of venture capital enterprises in the last few years. I have mentioned the Toronto-Dominion venture capital group. May I also mention Venta Investments, Charterhouse Canada Ltd., Canadian Enterprise Development Corporation, and Roynat Limited, a division of the Royal Bank.
The provinces have moved into this field as well with agencies to assist small business. There is the Ontario Development Corporation, Manitoba Development Corporation, Industrial Estates in Nova Scotia and so on. Clearly, the emergence of these provincial enterprises points up the failure of the Industrial Development Bank to fulfil the original mandate it was given when it was established 30 years ago.
If the Federal Business Development Bank is to be a success and really help small business, it must be shaken up from top to bottom and show genuine desire, through some direction from the minister, to move in a positive way to assist small business.
A case might be made that public funds are involved and they must be protected with adequate collateral, but look at what is at stake here. If you let your fingers do the walking through the yellow pages, as the advertisement
Federal Business Development Bank states, you will find that 90 per cent of the companies listed are small businesses. They create 50 per cent of Canada's gross national product, pay 50 per cent of all taxes collected by government and employ over 60 per cent of all the people working in Canada.
One cannot but wonder why they have been neglected so long by this government, but the reasons are obvious to those who seriously study the matter. Big business bureaucracy and the public bureaucracy work in close alliance. The goals of this alliance are essentially in conflict with the interests of most individual businessmen in Canada. This alliance increases the focus of public power and is responsible for the inequities in the free enterprise system.
A good case can be made in the rigidity of our tax system. The arrogance of the civil service in the application of Bill C-259, the Income Tax Act as amended in 1971, is evident. It is essentially a technocratic nightmare to the small businessman. Even large corporations have problems with the act, but at least they have the physical and financial resources to cope with it.
I would first like to see a small business enterprise defined and then some amendments to simplify the act so that the average businessman can understand it as it applies to his operation. I would like to see this as a separate section of the act, written in plain language, in terminology the average accountant can understand.
The measure of success the Federal Business Development Bank achieves will depend upon whether the minister is willing to go to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), and sell this idea. He must also seek out his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury), and have the tax form for small businesses simplified.
I am told that corporate managers and senior civil servants keep the same company. They have the same unfailing confidence in themselves that what they know and do is for the good of all people. However, the guts of the economy, the small businessman, has not been served. The people who really make this country go have been frustrated at every turn by a rigid and inflexible, arrogant bureaucracy. The proof is in the Bank of Canada figures which show the steady decline in the share of national income, as I quoted a few moments ago, from 10.5 per cent to 7.5 per cent over a period of 10 years or so.
While this and previous parliaments have wrestled with such weighty problems as bilingual guidelines, football legislation and all the social legislation that is leading us toward more state control, the small business enterprise has gone its way, still employing 60 per cent of the work force of this country, still paying more than 50 per cent of the taxes into the public treasury, and still accounting for 50 per cent of the gross national product.
Anyone in marketing and manufacturing will tell you that 80 per cent of the products on the shelves today will not be there in 15 years. They will have changed. New products will emerge, new ideas will come forth and new products will be created to fill the demands of the day.
Hardly a week goes by without a businessman contacting me to tell me of his inability to get venture capital to push a new product or idea. On my office desk are exam-
1810

April 26, 1974
Business of the House
pies of such innovations. One deals with a retrieval system for computers. It is a real breakthrough. It is a system that would immeasureably assist even the House of Commons and the Speaker. It allows information to be retrieved almost at will without the rigidity of a structured computer program.
Another deals with, of all things, dogs. A group of knowledgeable people have compiled courses for community colleges that will teach people the care and handling of dogs. These courses are presently being taught in four community colleges in Ontario. This group of people has inquiries from Japan, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, France and the United States, from people who want to use them in their education courses. They have produced a book and instruments that are absolutely unique. Fifteen more books are projected. This small group of people are being pressed by American publishers to sell publishing rights to them on a royalty basis. I am trying to get them started in a purely Canadian venture so they can export their products.
These are only two of the many examples that have come to my attention. Therefore, the question we in this parliament must face is whether we are going to urge the minister to make sure that the Federal Business Development Bank is flexible and is stripped of its rigidity so that it can respond to new ideas and use to the fullest the innovative talents one finds in the small business enterprise. May I call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

I might well say "if either of his or her parents is a Canadian citizen." It would please some women a lot if those words, "or her" had been inserted.
Time has gone by since September 28, 1970. On April 2, 1973, more than a year ago, the government replied to questions by my hon. colleague from Skeena (Mr. Howard) concerning this attitude toward a number of these recommendations. This was the reply given to the hon. member for Skeena with regard to that particular recommendation about Canadian citizenship:
The recommendation of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women to amend section 4 and 5 of the Canadian Citizenship Act to provide that a child born outside Canada is a natural-born Canadian if either of his parents is a Canadian citizen has been sympathetically considered and an opportunity for discussion will be given Members of the House shortly at the time the new citizenship bill or major amendments to the current act are introduced.
That was on April 2, 1973, and so far no legislation has been introduced to deal with this matter. The reply I have just quoted has been embodied in a pamphlet put out by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. The pamphlet is entitled "What has been done?". It sets out a list of the recommendations made by the Royal Commission and assesses what has been done with regard to each of them. With regard to the particular recommendation which is the subject of the proposal put forward in my bill, they say "Not implemented; amendments to the Citizenship Act are required."
It is three and a half years since the Report of the Royal Commission came out. In the meantime we have been getting letters from women who have been caught by this legislation. I have one letter I received from someone in a town in British Columbia about a year ago. I quote:
I should like to voice my support of your private member's bill to give Canadian married women living outside of Canada the same rights as men and unmarried mothers.
At the present time I am in the process of selling my business in Canada and will be moving to the United States to marry an American citizen.
I was born and raised a Canadian and intend keeping my citizenship. Several weeks ago I wrote to the immigration office to find out the status of my future children and was shocked to learn that I could not register them as Canadians.
Here is a letter from New York. This is a copy of a letter written a year ago to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). It puts the whole case very succinctly:
I should like to bring to your attention a matter which I believe falls within your area of responsibility, namely, the implementation of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada.
I am a natural-born citizen of Canada presently residing in America as a resident alien. My husband is an American citizen. On October 9, 1972,1 gave birth to a son, Peter Campbell Lichter, in New York City.
It is not possible to register him with the Canadian Consulate in New York, thereby awarding him dual nationality, because the Canadian Citizenship Act states that "A person born after the 31st day of December 1946 is a natural-born Canadian citizen ... if he is born outside of Canada elsewhere than on a Canadian ship, and (if) his father ... is a Canadian citizen ..."
Citizenship
The Canadian Bill of Rights, however, states that "It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religon or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely ... the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;"
The Canadian Citizenship Act would seem to be in direct contradiction to this aforementioned portion of the Bill of Rights: a woman clearly does not have equality as stated in the citizenship laws.
The Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada recognizes this inequality and states that "We believe Canadian men and women should have the same right to confer Canadian citizenship on their children ... Therefore, we recommend that sections 4 and 5 of the Canadian Citizenship Act be amended to provide that a child born outside Canada is a natural-born Canadian if either of his parents is a Canadian citizen ..." The greater importance attached to the citizenship of the father does not recognize the equal status of the citizenship of the mother".
Then the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women are embodied in the letter. This woman goes on to say:
The Citizenship Act has not been amended as of this date. As a citizen of Canada I am therefore bringing this to your attention in the hope that action may be taken on this specific recommendation of the Royal Commission. I look forward to hearing from you regarding this matter.
I should now like to read from a copy of another letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on November 15, 1973. It states in part:
I am a Canadian citizen, and I was always a resident of Canada until March 1972, when I became a resident of Switzerland. I am now engaged to be married to a Czechoslovakian who has been a Swiss resident since 1969, and whose nationality is presently defined as "stateless".
When I inquired at the Canadian Embassy in Berne what citizenship a child born to us in Switzerland could have, I was told it is unfortunate that I am a woman. It seems that the child would have the citizenship of the father, in this case "stateless", and that even then the mother's citizenship is not considered at all. I would appreciate knowing what steps are being taken by the government to change this appalling law.
So far we have had no evidence that steps are being taken, although from copies of answers to these letters which I have been I realize there are hopes that such legislation will be brought in. I expect that someone from the other side of the House will be speaking to indicate that the time is not far off. However, I should like to know when we may expect this legislation, what are the government's priorities, and when women will be brought up to equal status in a matter of this kind.
For the life of me I cannot understand why there should be so much red tape and delay. This is not a complicated matter. I am inclined to agree very firmly with the President of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, Dr. Katie Cooke, who in a recent press release said: "I get uneasy when what can be done easily is not done."
I want to say that I also become uneasy when what can be done easily is not done. I think this is something which could have been done easily a long time ago and which could be done easily at any time. I do not like to think of children of Canadians wandering around Switzerland as stateless individuals because their mother is regarded as an inferior citizen, without the right to confer Canadian citizenship. When we talk about Canadian nationalism and about developing our own industries and products in

I think that is stupid. I think it is time we began to realize that a Canadian woman should be in a position of equality with a Canadian man, no matter which country she happens to be in, and that she should have the same rights in respect of her children.
I could go on at greater length in respect of this matter but I shall not do so because I am led to believe quite a number of people would like to speak on this bill this afternoon. 1 should like to make my stopping now, in order to give these members a few minutes, contingent on their not saying that there will be legislation soon on this matter, because this is the answer we have received for a long time. speechtext:
I might mention to hon. members who are anxious to see this bill go to committee that there are some defects in the bill as currently drafted, and although this does not in any way reflect on the validity of the bill, perhaps the bill should be looked at in terms of the other problems which might arise if the bill were passed with its present wording.
I think I should add the caveat at this point that it is the accepted practice and tradition of this House that backbenchers do not speak for the government nor for any specific minister. While I intend to discuss many aspects of the Canadian Citizenship Act and many recommendations for change, neither the government nor the Secretary of State, who is the minister responsible for the Citizenship Act, should or could be in any way committed by what I might say this afternoon.
Twenty-seven years ago Canada became the first country in the Commonwealth to adopt a separate Citizenship Act which came into force on January 1, 1947. The bill was introduced by the Hon. Paul Martin, then secretary of state. Evidence of the changing concepts of citizenship can be found in the fact that there have been 61 amendments since that day.
There are a number of curiosities on anomalies in the present act, including, for example, the following. The period of residence to qualify for citizenship is shorter for wives than for husbands. This is regarded both as discrimination against and in favour of women, depending on
April 26, 1974

one's point of view. The father is designated as the "responsible parent" in applications for citizenship made on behalf of minors, unless the mother has legal custody or is the de facto guardian. The age of majority differs in the Canadian Elections Act and Citizenship Act, with the result that many persons between 18 and 21 are unable to vote because their non-citizen parents are ineligible to apply for citizenship on their behalf, as they are themselves, until they reach the age of majority specified in the Citizenship Act.
Twenty-seven years ago many people believed that there was a difference in the legal status of men and women and that the age of majority should be 21. Whether they were right or wrong is not at issue; what is important is that now, in 1974, 27 years and 61 amendments later, we should look to a Citizenship Act which reflects the thinking of our times and which will reflect the Canada of the 1970's.
Citizenship amounts to membership in the family called Canada, and it would seem to me that any new legislation would have to begin with the most basic consideration of all: shall we make it relatively easy or shall we make it relatively difficult for our brothers and sisters throughout the whole of humanity to join us in our Canadian family? I should think we would want to do everything possible to enable others to join us and to share in the pursuit of a decent life in a nation which is one of the most fortunate on earth.
It is perhaps we who are born here who "too easily forget that the accident of birth has entitled us to one of the most valued and desirable citizenships on earth. But we should remember this when we look to new legislation, that outside our borders stand men, women and children who ask only that they be allowed the opportunity to join us in Canada, to share with us in partnership the enormous resources of Canada and to live with us in respect ot one another and under the rule of law.
I hope we shall see legislation which reflects our willingness to encourage citizenship and not to make it difficult in any way. Neither marriage nor lack thereof should affect the rights of the newborn to Canadian citizenship. Children born abroad should not be required to undergo registration, and individuals who persistently live abroad should be able to pass on their citizenship rights generation by generation, provided only that they give evidence at our consular offices of a retained ability to speak either of our two official languages, and thus show an interest in their native homeland.
There should be no distinction in the law, as the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has quite rightly pointed out, between male and female. All distinctions between men and women which result in one or the other sex being placed at a disadvantage should be removed from the law. The legislation should and will, I hope, be so framed that all citizens, whether male or female, have the same rights under our law.
While the Royal Commission on the Status of Women recommended retroactivity in this regard, I would point out to the House that retroactivity is an extremely difficult concept in law and that often it is impossible to define exactly what may be the effects of such retroactivity. We can and should restore the status to women wher-
Citizenship
ever it may have been previously lost, provided there is no conflict with the private or the public interest. To go beyond that, however, would in all probability involve us in an unending examination of individual cases, making the application of our laws an almost ad hoc situation.
I think that in the Canada of the 1970's, the Citizenship Act should reflect both the law as found in other but relevant pieces of legislation and the changing circumstances in a world of virtually instant communications. If the age of capacity for voting is 18, then surely we must bring harmony to the Citizenship Act and reduce the age of capacity from 21 to 18 as well.
The length of residence is currently five years before application for Canadian citizenship can be made. Perhaps originally the period of five years had merit, but surely we can encourage those who ask to join our family. On this matter the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) has for several years presented private member's bills in an effort to reduce the five year period, and I will leave to him further comment in that regard.
I hope that we will ease the language requirements so that while on the one hand we indicate the desirability of a knowledge of one or the other of the two official languages of Canada, at the same time we provide exemptions in various categories. Then we should encourage those who come here with a limited knowledge or no knowledge of either of our two official languages by providing for them facilities for instruction in the language of their preference.
It is of the essence of citizenship that those who apply must accept the obligations which go with the rights. We should continue to insist that applicants for Canadian citizenship learn and understand our institutions of government and the role of law in our society. At the same time we need to develop systems of instruction and examination which provide the applicant not only with the opportunity to know our structures of society but to make use of education programs which will encourage his interest.
The entire subject of "good character" is a quicksand of shifting meaning and value. Whatever one individual might consider to be a matter of good character in a form that can be useful for the assessment of individual suitability for citizenship, another might consider irrelevant or even an invasion of privacy. The entire notion of good character should, I think, be simply disposed of and dispensed with for applicants who may have been charged with a deportable offence or who may be subject to deportation following conviction for such an offence.
In days gone by, perhaps it was useful to have the posting of an application for citizenship in the office of the clerk of the court for the period of three months before the court considered the application. Posting simply has no meaning in reality today and should be completely eliminated.
We should be done with the business of renunciation of foreign nationality. Nationality law of various countries either applies the principle that a national cannot divest himself of nationality by the act of renunciation without the consent of the state, or that voluntary acquisition of foreign nationality results automatically in loss of citizen-

April 26, 1974
Citizenship
ship. In the one case, therefore, a declaration of renunciation takes no effect, while in the other case it is superfluous.
We should consider naturalization to be a right, not a privilege. Naturalization, resumption, retention and renunciation should altogether form the right of the applicant, with of course exceptions for special cases. This would prevent arbitrary exercise of executive authority and discrimination unfounded in our laws.
We will need to preserve ministerial discretion for many reasons, but essentially to protect Canada and the Canadian public in special cases which our law may not pursue.
We will want to retain our citizenship court and judge who provide both the image and the substance of the importance of the occasion in terms of its impact on the individual applicant.
I said earlier that I cannot, of course, speak for either the government or the minister responsible in this regard, but I very much hope that parliament will be able to give serious consideration to the manner by which an individual may lose his Canadian citizenship, and that I hope this will be restricted to one case only-the voluntary decision of that individual who seeks citizenship in another jurisdiction.
I hope that both parliament and the people of Canada will recognize the maturing of our nation and do away with the preferential treatment of British subjects. The Canadian Citizenship Act now excuses British subjects from appearance before a court, thus exempting them from any effective examination and creating what is felt by many immigrants of other backgrounds to be an invidious distinction. Although the system of preferential treatment may have had some logic based upon language, similarity of political systems, historical association and the reciprocal benefits, all in the past, all those grounds for preference can be shown today to be equally applicable to many other national groups. In effect, this is a discriminatory process in the Canada of the 1970's. It establishes a class of people based upon national origin rather than upon individual worth. At its worst, it is insulting to those who are of other than British origin and has no foundation either in logic or in moral value. I would go further and point out that it is my belief that there are few applicants for citizenship of British origin who in this day and age would ask for preferential treatment. For them to do so or for us to continue such treatment amounts to moral discrimination which is distasteful and totally unfounded.
At the same time, in terms of the Canadian Citizenship Act we should abandon the expression "British subject status", which is taken for purposes of federal legislation to include Canadian citizens, nationals of the Commonwealth countries and the republic of Eire. British subject status is a term entirely derivative from citizenship and has no independent reality whatsoever. The term is widely misunderstood and often resented or considered inappropriate in an independent country such as ours. The term is virtually meaningless, but because it appears in other federal legislation one may hope that the Citizenship Act will be amended in such a manner as to avoid confusion or conflict with other legislation, but at the same time remove this concept from our law of citizenship.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not occupy too many minutes in the House this afternoon, but I have stood on a number of other occasions for this principle of equal rights for women before the law. I have done so on the matter of pensions and I do so again here.
I do also having had some experience with the administration of this particular act from the very day of its inception. It is a difficult act to administer, particularly abroad. I agree fully with the intent of the amendment put before us in Bill C-110. I have a suggestion to make in order to avoid another discriminatory use which is forced upon us, I suppose, because of the nature of the English language. At any rate, it does not appear quite the same in French, hopefully because of the nature of the French language. I would say that instead of saying "his father" or "his mother", the Act should say "the father" or "the mother" of the child at the time of its birth.
There is one other matter in this bill which I think we should not lose sight of. The hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) did mention the extraordinary anomaly that was created by the fact that if one of the parents, actually the citizen-giving parent under the present Canadian law, happened to be a stateless person, he therefore transferred statelessness upon the child. This is, of course, completely unacceptable to any human being.
The other thing we must remember is that in the suggested proposal put forward here we run the risk of conferring dual nationality upon the child because the father and the mother might, under separate laws relating to the country of their own nationality, each confer a nationality upon the child. I suggest, therefore, that there might be a further amendment toward the end of that particular clause, or in the clause relating to the statement or declaration that must be made by the child under the Canadian law in deciding which nationality he shall choose, if by any chance he should be a dual national, either at the age of 21 or 18, as suggested by the previous speaker.
Some provision ought to be made under the law that the child should as a matter of right be informed by the government of Canada that he should make his declaration, and should be informed at least a year prior to the date when he must make that decision. Children and parents too, it has been my experience, often forget this requirement. Having registered their child at the consolate they think as a matter of course he is going to be a Canadian, but in the case of a dual national it is necessary for him to decide whether he is to be Canadian or some other nationality. Therefore I think we must try, in addition to the suggestions made here, and in the context of this particular amendment, to make provision for that child to be notified prior to the date that he must declare his intention to renounce one of his citizenships.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in this debate on Bill
Citizenship
C-110 today. I want first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for having introduced this bill. 1 want that hon. member to know that even if her bill were not to reach the committee stage it will have nevertheless permitted certain members of this House to bring once more out into the open the fact that discrimination against women does exist in many of our Canadian laws, and that it is time this should be corrected.

Mr. Speaker, after reading sections 4 to 15 of the Citizenship Act one has the clear impression that the act gives a child born out of wedlock outside Canada to a Canadian mother the possibility to become a Canadian citizen but that same act denies a child born to a wed mother marrying a foreigner the same privileges as those extended to an illegitimate child.
Mr. Speaker, let me read, from that section which had me puzzled:
A person born after the 31st day of December... if he is born in Canada is a Canadian citizen, or if he is born outside of Canada, and (i) his father, or in the case of a child born out of wedlock, his mother, at the time of that person's birth, is a Canadian citizen,...
So, as I said before, if a Canadian marrying a foreigner gives birth to a child abroad and if the marriage fails afterwards and she wants to come back to this country the child is not a Canadian citizen.
On the other hand, section 5(2) states that:
A child born to a Canadian father or a Canadian mother and an unknown father has three years after his 21st birthday to decide whether he wants to retain his citizenship or give it up. He has a choice. But, as I already said, if a child is born to a Canadian mother marrying a foreigner who afterwards leaves her husband, if that child wants to become a Canadian citizen, it is absolutely impossible. On the other hand, section 6 states that on his 21st birthday such a child may file a petition for resumption of Canadian citizenship, and the minister has the necessary discretion to either approve or reject that petition.
Once again, that privilege exists for a child born to a Canadian father and a child born out of wedlock. After reading that act one has the impression that it favours birth out of wedlock for those living abroad, and that does not make sense. Section 7 states:
Every foundling, who is or was first found as a deserted infant in Canada,...
-is considered a Canadian citizen. I have nothing against it. On the contrary, it is quite commendable but that foundling who has the Canadian citizenship ipso facto can be the child of foreigners only visiting in Canada, the child of parents who would not have the status of British subject, but having been found in Canada he becomes a Canadian citizen. On the other hand, if a Canadian woman living abroad, separated from her husband but with two children, wishes to return to her country, her children do not have Canadian citizenship. What nonsense!
I wondered if my interpretation of the legislation was wrong and thought that the minister surely had the discretion to grant citizenship to children such as the above-mentioned. I referred first to the clauses dealing with the minister's discretion and then to section 10. And I said to

April 26, 1974
Citizenship
myself: Now, the minister can, at his discretion, grant a citizenship certificate to anyone who is not a Canadian citizen and makes an application after 21 years of age. I said: Fair enough. But what about the spouse of a Canadian citizen residing in Canada? It is still impossible for the child of such a union to become a Canadian citizen. What about the person who has been residing in Canada for at least 12 to 18 months immediately preceding the application date? How is it possible to enforce the law? No clause applies to such cases.
Section 10(4) reads and I quote:
The Minister may, in his discretion, grant a certificate of citizenship...
Paragraph (c) states-
... a British subject who was born elsewhere than in Canada or on a Canadian ship, whose father, or in the case of a person born out of wedlock...
Once more, if a woman marries a foreigner who has children and whose marriage is afterwards dissolved, or who is simply legally separated, her children are not yet recognized as Canadian citizens.
In all the sections dealing with the minister's discretion, none provides for the case I just mentioned.
Again, I hope I am mistaken, because if the legislators have really dreamed up such legislation, it would be about time to amend it. Now, Mr. Speaker, far from objecting to the bill of the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), I am totally in favour of it, even of her amendment.
I repeat in English, I am totally in favour of such an amendment. However, I am told that the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) will be introducing legislation to amend this act so that, among many things, men and women will be given equal status in this country.
In addition to this, an onmibus bill on the status of women will be placed before the House in the near future, a bill which will remove from a number of other acts provisions which are presently prejudicial to women.

We know that this legislation is not the only one which is discriminating against women. It is strangely similar to section 12(1) (b) of the Indian Act. An Indian man, whether he has 25 or 50 per cent Indian blood, can marry, for instance, a cabaret dancer from Texas with four or five kids who become ipso facto full-fledged Indians. But an Indian woman who marries a white man and who is separated from her husband, through judicial separation or through divorce, cannot go back to the Indian reserve, even if she is 100 per cent Indian. What's more, she cannot be buried in her ancestors' cemetery. Here is another piece of legislation discriminating very much against women. Fortunately, an onmibus bill on the status of women will be brought in soon.

Fortunate indeed are the women of Canada that Canadian legislators are, like St. Paul on the road to Damascus, finally beginning "to see the light."

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Prud'homme (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CITIZENSHIP FOR CHILD OF CANADIAN BORN OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the other members, of course, I have read with great interest the bill introduced by the member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis).
Surely, if we recognize that all Canadian citizens are equal before the law and entitled to an equal treatment, it goes without saying that the hon. member's bill should become part of the Canadian statutes. The Canadian Citizenship Act should be amended.
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, you reminded my colleague from Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker), in all fairness, that he was perhaps getting away from the matter before us, but on second thought, I must say that if the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway seeks amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act, we must surely be given some leeway. On the subject of amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act, one could say that this legislation is unfair in many ways.
That was what my colleague meant when he said, in agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway, that we should amend the Canadian Citizenship Act.
A great many other sections of the Canadian Citizenship Act should have been amended long ago. It is in this vein that my colleague spoke at the outset of his remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that we see a great many cases of injustice in Canada. At least for the time being, the Women's Lib movement appears to me to be going astray. Nevertheless, I think I can say in another are a "equal pay for equal work". I may be out of order, but this example merely goes to prove that there is injustice everywhere. Moreover, the hon. member is perfectly aware that if a woman can do the job of a man, she should normally get the same pay; if a man can make a Canadian citizen of his child, I do not see why a woman could not.
I can think of all kinds of other amendments, not to break the rules but to show that the Citizenship Act should be amended, but not bit by bit. I shall refer to a bill that I already introduced. I think that my memory serves me right because I have here the papers for December 18, 1970, March 2, 1972, June 1973, and March 12, 1974, when I asked that the time limit for obtaining Canadian citizenship be reduced from five to three years. This was an amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act, and I shall not dwell on the matter because it will eventually be discussed in the House.
The hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) will agree that it is not bit by bit that we should obtain this from the government-because I am not one of its members; I sit on the government side, but I am not a cabinet member-but that we should stop the debate before five o'clock and refer this bill to the committee and amend the Canadian Citizenship Act. In my opinion, this is not what we want to do in the House. I am not interested in taking everything the government offers, because I know what we could obtain, and in accepting the scraps it gives us to soothe us. For my part, I have been asking for
April 26, 1974

something for four years, and it is time a decision were made.
The hon. member is proposing an amendment to a section of the act, namely section 5(l)(b)(i), and the government is saying: these amendments have been proposed for so many years that we shall give in. Since there are several amendments proposed to the Canadian Citizenship Act, as the hon. member knows from the list of private members' bills, we can see that there is considerable interest in amending the Canadian Citizenship Act.
I know my hon. colleague in the official opposition does not agree that we should take steps to make all citizens equal before the law.
I am a Canadian of French extraction and I do not seek greater rights than those of English Canadians, but I would not accept that English-speaking Canadians should have rights I would be deprived of. I think that we are all equal before the law and we should all be considered as such. That is why even though I do not want to scare anybody nor start a futile argument, I wonder about restrictions applicable to citizens who are said to be British. I do not see why those people should be treated any differently from Ukrainian, Polish, Italian, Greek, French or English Canadians. I think that if all citizens are to be equal before the law ... I do not wish to start a useless argument with people more aware of the status fo British citizenship. Besides, I would be ready to uphold that opinion before any group in Canada, whether it be the Royalist League of Canada or any other movement. If we believe that all citizens are equal before the law, it is only normal for all of us to be treated equally.
I agree, of course, with the bill introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), except that I am wondering about the legislator's intention.
I cannot understand how legislators well briefed by the Department of Justice's legal advisors could include in the Canadian citizenship Act such an amendment or such a limitation.
I am therefore wondering what was the legislator's intention. Did he want to avoid something? I did not get any answer. The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) will eventually introduce a bill. I therefore urge the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, all my colleagues who are interested in the Canadian Citizenship Act, members from the official opposition, members from the Social Credit party of Canada to get together so as to wrench out of the government of the House leader a piece of legislation that has been drafted for many years. I do not wish to divulge secrets I came to know as parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State, but I know that a piece of legislation has been in the making for many years. I know that legislation is now ready. What remains to be done now is to find in the House the right moment to table a bill that will not only meet with the wishes of the very distinguished member for Vancouver Kingsway, but that will also provide Canada with a modern statute in keeping with our time without rejecting what has been done in the past.
In the past, citizens of a different racial origin were treated differently. It was the Canadian history of the
Citizenship
past. I see that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) is looking straight at me. Maybe there was some reason then, historical reasons, to treat citizens differently, but like all the others, he might perhaps join the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway in order that finally we might have a modern act, truly Canadian rather than French Canadian, English Canadian, multiculturally Canadian or Ukrainian. This would be an act respecting modern Canadian citizenship whereby everyone would receive equal treatment. No special treatment would be afforded a married citizen without his wife getting the same treatment whether she is abroad or from any ethnic group or what have you.
I regret that my time is up, but I would not want to be the last member in this House to speak on the matter. I know that in this respect I will wholeheartedly co-operate with the very distinguished member for Vancouver Kingsway in order that together we may extract from the government, because I feel there will be ample time for that until the end of the session and next fall, that we may get under this government a modern act on Canadian citizenship.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CITIZENSHIP FOR CHILD OF CANADIAN BORN OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in this debate and I strongly support the remarks of the previous speaker. I think that if the bill is studied and debated seriously, the question raised in particular by the honourable member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), i.e. that of multinationality, must be examined deeply.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on this matter.
There are many people who, due to legal conflicts in this regard have several nationalities. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, the honourable member for Esquimalt-Saanich mentioned the fact that a person might happen to hold two or more nationalities. And I am thinking particularly about American or Israelite parents, for instance, who could be in Canada and whose child could have three nationalities, Americain, Israelite and Canadian.
Most countries do not tolerate such an arrangement and multi-nationality is not recognized, but here in Canada, the existing legislation seems to have been written for this purpose, i.e. we recognize the right to Canadian nationality of the person born in Canada and, in certain cases, of persons whose father or son is Canadian.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) when she proposes a very important amendment to the present act which would entitle to citizenship any child born in whatever way from a Canadian father or mother. I would like this debate to be quick and that the government deemr it convenient to propose a complete bill which would give us the chance to discuss all the problems involved in this question which is obviously quite important.
